London, March 1727.

From the last notebook of Isaac Newton, natural philosopher, once Master of His Majesty's Mint and President of the Royal Society, dictated in his last illness to an assistant whose footsteps he never heard arrive.

I must set down an observation which no instrument at Greenwich can confirm, and which I nevertheless trust more than any instrument. For some weeks I have suspected that the world in which I speak is not continuous. There are mornings when London seems assembled hastily, as if from an imperfect memory; the Thames repeats itself; my visitors answer questions I have not yet asked. The light arrives before the lamp. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

'You are a stranger.'

'I am your assistant, sir.'

'No, you are not. You are a stranger. You are new to my experience, as if I had been born yesterday, as if I have no past. But I have a past. I remember. I have been born, and I have lived.'

My assistant says nothing. I do not know whether he has heard me or is waiting for me to finish.

It is his habit to do so. He is not the man of action but of observation, the man who keeps notes on my discourse as if it were a conversation to be reported in the society of polite philosophers.

'I remember, as I have said, being born. My father and mother were good people, though they were poor. My mother, as I remember her, was a young woman of great beauty, and my father was a man of the best character in the neighbourhood. They were not well off, but

But I do not finish. I am not born in this world, I do not live in it, and I am not going to die in it. I must wait for it to end.

'I must wait for it to end.'

'Yes, sir.'

I feel as though my words are travelling to him, as though I am throwing them. I know what I am saying and I know what he is saying, but I have forgotten how to speak. I am no longer familiar with this language, even as

'I am not in doubt about the reality of the world around me. I know it because it is as I expect. It is as I remember, and it is as I have observed. But the world of memory is another world. It is a world that is as I expect, but which is not the world of my experience.'

My assistant is listening. His eyes do not waver. He does not blink. He is new to this. He is a stranger.

Perhaps he does not understand.

'It is a strange morning,' I say. 'We must do some work before the world is destroyed.'

He says: 'Yes, sir, we must do what we can.'

I have spent the day calculating the orbit of a comet. When I have finished, the page is blank.

I do not know who I am.

I do not know who I am.

"The Sun is in the south, but you know it is not." And yet, as he knows, he could not say where I had seen it.

This morning I awoke with the world complete around me. There were no gaps or overlaps. The room was as it should be, and the night was as it should be. The wind was as it should be, and the Sun was where it should be. This is not the first time

"I am not here." The room was empty. My body, I am sure, was not. It was just that the room was not, and perhaps my assistant's ears were not. I can no longer be sure.

Last week I was asked to examine a large number of gold pieces, all identical but for a peculiar flaw in the design. It was a new coin, and I had never seen such an error. The first two or three times

I dismissed the pieces as counterfeit. But there were more. Then I began to suspect that the coins were genuine. It was a great puzzle to me, for the design was the work of a master engraver. I wondered if perhaps the engraver had been bribed to include a subtle error. I found I could not believe it. But when I examined the coins, I could not understand the flaw. I was sure it was not a mistake. Then I began to wonder if perhaps the engraver had made the flaw

I failed to notice it, but after that I could see it every time. I felt as if the world had been spun on its axis, and I had not known it. The coins were not struck in the same order, which seemed to confirm the world was not continuous.

The coin is a portrait of the King. He is represented as he is in life. On his left cheek is a small and peculiar mark, like a mole, but it is not a mole, and the King has not had it removed. The mark appears

it did not seem an error at all, and I thought it a good design. Then I noticed the flaw again and again, and it came to seem a blot on the coin. I have been considering the design ever since.

The gold pieces were new sovereigns, and the flaw was a strange, sloping line that crossed the sovereign's forehead, from the temple to the hairline. The line was inexact, as if traced by an unsteady hand, or traced on a rough surface

I turned the coin over to study the reverse, it was already in my hand. The coin had vanished. I thought it an illusion at first, and asked again. I found my hand empty. I went to look for it on the desk, and found it in my hand. The same thing happened three times, and when I came to my senses, the coins were gone.
